guide.title: Travel guide
guide.text: Everything you need to know before your trip.

items.title: Arriving
items.text: Most travelers arrive at Manas International Airport (FRU) in Bishkek or Osh Airport (OSS). Taxi apps work in both cities.

items.title: Shared taxis & marshrutkas
items.text: Minibuses (marshrutkas) and shared taxis connect all towns cheaply. In Bishkek they leave from the Western and Eastern bus stations.

items.title: Car with driver
items.text: For remote places like Song-Kul or Kel-Suu, hire a 4x4 with a driver through a local tour company or CBT office.

items.title: Domestic flights
items.text: Flights between Bishkek and Osh take about 1 hour and save a long 10–12 hour drive.

items.title: Summer (June–September)
items.text: The main season. High passes and jailoos are open, yurt camps work, and Issyk-Kul is warm enough for swimming.

items.title: Spring (April–May)
items.text: Green valleys and blooming hills, great for canyons and lower hikes. High mountains still have snow.

items.title: Autumn (September–October)
items.text: Golden forests, clear skies and walnut harvest in Arslanbob. Nights get cold in the mountains.

items.title: Winter (December–March)
items.text: Skiing in Karakol and around Bishkek, hot springs and snowy landscapes. Many high roads are closed.

items.title: Hospitality
items.text: Guests are honored. If invited for tea, accept at least one cup; bread (nan) should never be put upside down or thrown away.

items.title: In a yurt
items.text: The place opposite the door (tör) is for honored guests. Don't step on the threshold and take off your shoes inside.

items.title: Dress
items.text: Casual clothes are fine in cities. Dress modestly at mosques, shrines and in rural villages.

items.title: Language
items.text: Kyrgyz and Russian are official. A few words help a lot: Salamatsyzby (hello), Rakhmat (thank you).

items.title: Visa
items.text: Citizens of many countries can visit visa-free for up to 60 days. Always check the latest rules before you travel.

items.title: Money
items.text: The currency is the Kyrgyz som (KGS). Cards work in cities; carry cash for villages, yurt camps and markets.

items.title: SIM & internet
items.text: Buy a local SIM (Beeline, MegaCom, O!) at the airport with your passport. Mobile internet is cheap and fast in towns.

items.title: Safety
items.text: Kyrgyzstan is generally safe. In the mountains, tell someone your plan, watch the weather and consider a guide for high treks.

items.title: Border zones
items.text: Areas near the Chinese and Tajik borders (e.g. Kel-Suu, Chatyr-Kul) need a border-zone permit arranged in advance.

about.title: About Kyrgyzstan
about.text: A mountainous country in the heart of Central Asia, on the ancient Silk Road.

sections.title: Land of mountains
sections.text: The Tien Shan and Pamir-Alay ranges cover more than 90% of Kyrgyzstan. Glaciers feed thousands of rivers and lakes, and summer pastures (jailoo) stretch across high plateaus where herders still move with their animals.

sections.title: History on the Silk Road
sections.text: For centuries caravans crossed this land between China and the West. Cities like Balasagun, Osh and Uzgen flourished, leaving towers, caravanserais and petroglyphs. Kyrgyzstan became an independent republic in 1991.

sections.title: Nomadic heritage
sections.text: The yurt (boz üy) is the symbol of Kyrgyz culture — its crown (tündük) is even on the national flag. Horse games like kok-boru, felt carpets (shyrdak), the white kalpak hat and the World Nomad Games keep traditions alive.

sections.title: The epic of Manas
sections.text: The epic of Manas tells the story of the hero who united the Kyrgyz tribes. It is one of the longest epic poems in the world and is recited by storytellers called manaschy.

sections.title: Food
sections.text: Try beshbarmak (noodles with meat), plov, lagman, manty, samsa from a tandoor oven, fresh boorsok and drinks like kymyz (fermented mare's milk) and maksym.
